To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the sensitivity of screening mammograms for the detection of breast cancer is higher in women who have a higher body weight than in those who are leaner; (ii) the sensitivity for the detection of invasive cancer is higher in overweight and obese women than in lean women; (iii) the sensitivity for detection of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is similar in all body mass index (BMI) groups;
1) The sensitivity of screening mammograms for detecting invasive cancer is 90% and for detecting DCIS it is 50%.

1. The sensitivity of mammography screening in women aged 40-49 years is lower than the sensitivity in older women; and 2. The sensitivity of screening is lower in overweight women than in normal-weight women.

the effects of the body weight of a patient on the results of screening mammography and on the sensitivity of screening mammograms.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
screening mammography has a sensitivity of approximately 80% and specificity of approximately 90% for the detection of invasive breast cancer.
there is a significant association between BMI and the sensitivity of mammography, and that this association is independent of other risk factors.
the evidence is insufficient to conclude that the use of mammography in women aged 40 to 49 years reduces the mortality from breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bodyweight is a significant predictor of the sensitivity of screening mammogram, but the relationship is not linear.
the results of the current study suggest a dose-dependent association between body weight and sensitivity of mammographic screening, which is in line with the results of other studies.
the sensitivity of mammography is significantly reduced in women with a body mass index (BMI) greater than or equal to 30.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of body weight on screening mammography sensitivity is small, and the effect is not different for women with dense versus fatty breasts.
the sensitivity and specificity of screening mammography are not constant across all women, but are dependent on a woman's body mass index.
women who are overweight or obese should not assume that their increased risk for breast cancer will be detected by screening mammography.
